frames.narration: Listings arrive at 500 a second. Each goes into a memory buffer, and into a write-ahead log so a crash cannot lose it. Nothing is searchable yet.
A refresh every second turns the buffer into a new small segment and opens it to searches. A new listing now waits 500 ms on average, 950 ms at worst.
A segment is never edited. A search reads every segment and merges the answers, so each refresh adds a little cost to every query.
Break it: refresh every 100 ms to be fresher (50 ms wait), and with no merging the index ends with 1,200 segments. Every query now looks in all 1,200.
A merge thread combines 10 segments of similar size into one bigger segment, in the background. The count stays in a band: a peak of 27 and 3 at the end for the same 100 ms refresh.

Merging has a price: it rewrites documents already on disk. At a 100 ms refresh, 224,465 documents are written for 60,000 that arrived, a write amplification of 3.74. Deleted copies are dropped in the rewrite.

At the other extreme, a 30 s refresh costs almost nothing to write (1.00) but a new listing waits 15,000 ms on average. Refresh interval is freshness against segment count; merge threshold is segment count against rewriting.
